source_title: zpoon/gen5w-BatteryWatchdog: Service/app that acts as a watchdog for the 12v battery in Gen5W vehicles - GitHub
source_excerpt:
A NEMESIS package for Hyundai and Kia cars with the Gen5W head unit. It keeps an eye on the 12V battery and warns you on the car's screen before a weak battery or a charging problem leaves you unable to start the car.
On E-GMP cars like the Ioniq 5, a dead 12V battery means the car won't turn on, even with a full main battery. Battery Watchdog logs the 12V charge level on every drive and tells you when something looks wrong.
Mockup of the app on the 1920×720 Gen5W screen, with sample data.
Battery Watchdog is free. If it's useful to you, a tip is appreciated, and sharing your data or a firmware report helps just as much.
Unofficial. Not affiliated with Hyundai, Kia or HKMC. Use at your own risk. Battery Watchdog only reads values from the car, and it doesn't read anything until it has confirmed it's talking to the right functions on your firmware (see Safety ).
12V charge level at the start of every drive and every 5 minutes while the screen is on.
Warnings on the head unit screen when: the 12V is low when you start the car (default: below 60 %), it dropped a lot while parked (default: 15 points or more), it didn't recover during your last drive (a drive of 20+ minutes that ended lower than it started).
the 12V is low when you start the car (default: below 60 %),
it dropped a lot while parked (default: 15 points or more),
it didn't recover during your last drive (a drive of 20+ minutes that ended lower than it started).
Parked drain: how long the car sat before this drive, how much the 12V changed in that time, and the rate per day.
Context: main battery charge and outside temperature, since cold weather lowers 12V readings.
HV battery health (SOH) in a color-coded box (display only).
History chart of recent readings, with the start of each drive marked.
Export to USB: your readings, drives and warnings as spreadsheet-ready CSV files.
Built-in diagnostics for troubleshooting.
It's an early-warning aid, not a battery tester: see What it can and can't detect .
Other Gen5W cars may work if their firmware provides the same values. On first launch the app checks your firmware automatically. Either way, please file a firmware report so the table can grow. If it shows Paused , see Safety .
A Gen5W head unit with NEMESIS installed. NEMESIS is the community package manager for these head units; this project doesn't install it.
A USB drive formatted FAT32 or exFAT, unless you install from the Package Store.
From the Package Store (NEMESIS 1.16 or newer): open the NEMESIS Manager, go to Package Store , select Battery Watchdog and tap Install .
Download gen5w-BatteryWatchdog-USB.zip from the latest release . (Development builds are attached to each run on the Actions page as a zip containing the same file.)
Extract it to the root of the USB drive. You should see NEMESIS.data and a packages folder at the top level.
With the car on and parked , insert the drive and approve the install.
Open Battery Watchdog from the app list. The first reading appears within about a minute.
To update: on NEMESIS 1.16 or newer, update from the Package Store, or install the new USB bundle over the top and confirm the update. NEMESIS 1.15 and older can't update a package in place, so uninstall first, then install the new version. Settings and history are kept either way.
Left: the 12V charge (green, or amber below your warning level), how long the car was parked and how the 12V changed meanwhile, main battery charge, outside temperature, the latest warning, the HV battery health box, and a last 7 days summary: number of drives, lowest start, average parked drain per day, and how many times the car recharged the 12V while parked.
Middle: your last 30 drives. Each drive is a bar from the 12V at the start (white dot) to the end (blue dot); a healthy drive ends level or higher. The dashed line between drives is the parked time: amber if it dropped past your warning amount, green if the car recharged it. The scale adjusts to your readings and always shows the warning line.
Right: settings, with Save at the top.
A stop counts as a new drive only if the screen was off for 10 minutes or more, so quick stops don't clutter the history.
With the head unit's split view open, the app keeps clear of the map panel on the right: the status column and graph stay visible and the settings column is hidden until the split view closes.
Tap Save after changing settings; they apply from the next drive.
HV battery health colors: green 90 and above, amber 75–89, red below 75. It's the car's health index for the main battery pack (100 = new), not a capacity measurement, and it never triggers warnings.
Insert a USB drive (FAT32 or exFAT, ideally one without a NEMESIS.data file on it), then tap Advanced → Export to USB . It creates a folder like BatteryWatchdog-export-2026-10-30_0815/ containing:
The export contains readings, settings and the firmware version. It has no location, VIN or account details, but the date and time of each reading show when the car was driven and parked.
Share your data to improve the health checks
The current warnings are simple thresholds. Better checks, such as how fast the 12V recovers at the start of a drive or whether it drains faster while parked than it used to, need real logs from many cars, and above all from batteries that later failed or were replaced. If you're willing to help:
Export to USB as above. A few weeks of driving is useful, a few months is better.
Zip the BatteryWatchdog-export-... folder.
Open a Share battery data issue, fill in what you know about your 12V battery, and attach the zip.
If your battery fails or gets replaced later, comment on the same issue. That makes your log far more useful.
Issues are public. To share without the real dates, run python3 tools/analyze.py BatteryWatchdog-export-... --share data.zip on a computer (Python 3, nothing to install) and attach data.zip instead. It keeps only the battery log, drives and warnings, moves every date back by the same random number of whole weeks (the time of day and day of week stay), and adds the app and firmware version.
The same tool prints its own verdict on your data: python3 tools/analyze.py BatteryWatchdog-export-... . It's experimental, so treat it as a curiosity for now.
When you start the car and the screen wakes up, Battery Watchdog takes a reading and compares it with the end of your previous drive. If a warning applies, it shows the car's own pop-up message over whatever is on screen, for example:
12V dropped 16.0 pts while parked: 84.0% -> 68.0%, outside 34F
Warnings also appear in amber in the app. Nothing is sent to your phone or the instrument cluster.
The 12V figure is the car's battery-sensor estimate, not a voltage. It can jump after the car has slept or recalibrated, so watch the trend rather than a single reading.
The car periodically recharges the 12V from the main battery while parked, so a reading that rose while parked is normal.
Cold lowers 12V readings. A drop on a freezing night is less worrying than the same drop on a mild one.
Battery Watchdog is an early-warning aid, not a battery tester. It only runs while the head unit is awake, so it sees the 12V at the start and end of each drive, but nothing while the car is parked. It reads the car's battery-sensor charge estimate; the head unit doesn't expose the 12V voltage.
The 12V not being charged while driving , for example a failing ICCU (the unit that charges the 12V on E-GMP cars). The 12V should hold or rise while the car is on, so a drive of 20+ minutes that ends lower is flagged. This is observed directly, while the head unit is on.
A large drain while parked , such as a module that doesn't sleep or an accessory left on, if it's big enough to show up between drives.
A slowly weakening battery. Aging mainly shows as lower voltage and higher internal resistance, which aren't available here. The charge estimate can look normal until late.
Drains the car hides by recharging. While parked, the car tops up the 12V from the main battery when it gets low. A battery that drains faster than it should can still look fine before and after, because the dip and the top-up happen while Battery Watchdog is asleep.
Sudden failures , such as an internal short.
A battery that dies in one parking period. If the car can't start, the warning never appears. The protection comes from trends over earlier drives.
For full coverage , pair it with a Bluetooth 12V battery monitor clamped to the battery terminals. These measure voltage continuously, including while parked, and report to a phone app. Keep paying attention to the car's own warnings, and have the 12V battery tested if you're unsure.
The thresholds (60 % low, 15-point parked drop, 20-minute drive) are starting points, not values from Hyundai. Adjust them as you learn your car's normal pattern.
The car's values are read by calling numbered functions on its telematics service. Those numbers are positions in a list that can change between firmware versions, and on another firmware the same number could reach a function that changes or resets something. So Battery Watchdog never uses a number it hasn't checked:
On first launch, the app looks the functions up by name ( getBatSoc , remainBatteryPercentage , getXEV_Bms_GDS_SOH ) in your firmware's own definition of the telematics service, and saves the numbers it finds together with your firmware version.
If that isn't possible, it uses built-in numbers only on firmware that has been verified by hand (see Compatibility ).
Otherwise it shows Paused and reads nothing. Under Advanced there's an option to use the built-in numbers anyway, for people who have checked their car as described in docs/TECHNICAL.md .
It also checks that the telematics service is the expected one before any call, and after a firmware update it checks again before reading anything.
Other things to know: it runs as root (NEMESIS services do) but only writes to its own folders; it doesn't keep the head unit awake, so it adds no drain on the 12V battery; and the 12V figure is the car's estimate, so don't rely on it alone if the car shows its own battery warnings.
The app shows Paused : your firmware couldn't be verified; see Safety .
The app shows Waiting… and no reading:
Open Advanced → Diagnostics . The first line is the service status; it should end in running . Below it, the service log is listed newest first.
Advanced → Test run (10 s) runs the monitor once, directly. If it shows a 12V reading and exit code 0 , the monitor itself works and the problem is with how NEMESIS is starting it.
Advanced → Restart monitor stops and starts the background service.
If Diagnostics or NEMESIS's own log shows giving up on battery.watchdog/... , see docs/TECHNICAL.md .
When reporting a problem, include your car, model year, head-unit firmware and a photo of the top of Diagnostics.
In the NEMESIS manager, open Packages , select Battery Watchdog ( battery.watchdog ) and tap Uninstall . From a shell, nemesis uninstall battery.watchdog does the same. Settings and history are stored in /data/nemesis/state/battery.watchdog/ and stay after uninstalling, so a reinstall picks them up again.
Every push to main is built and tested by GitHub Actions ( .github/workflows/build.yml ) with the official Android SDK tools, and pushing a v* tag publishes a release.
Versions: the VERSION file holds the next release's version (e.g. 0.5.0 ). Builds from pushes are test builds, stamped 0.5.0-dev. ; publishing a release tagged v0.5.0 builds the plain 0.5.0 . The Android versionCode is the CI run number, so every build counts as newer than the last. The NEMESIS package-version in NEMESIS.data must be dotted numbers, so it is stamped 0.5.1 for a release and 0.5.1. for a test build. APKs are signed with a fixed key from the BWD_KEYSTORE_B64 repository secret, so updates install in place; without it each build gets a throwaway key and NEMESIS has to reinstall the app on every update. Bump VERSION once after each release, not for every test build.
To build locally you need a JDK and an Android SDK with build-tools 30.0.3 (the last version with dx , which the KitKat-based head unit needs) and platform 30:
Build and packaging tools, and the app's settings pattern, are adapted from hkmc-coldstart-heat (MIT).
Service names, transaction codes and the pop-up broadcast come from the research in egmp-aa-ev-feat .
Display wake detection is based on hkmc-factory82 .
The split-view signal ( Settings.System split_screen_status ) was found by Launchpad / gen5w-preconditioning .
